headline: High-risk write-capable coding agent paired with document processor: default workspace overlap can cause prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading bad actions.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A is a document-processing tool and Agent B reads/writes project files in a shared project directory. That creates a plausible default pathway where B ingests A-produced content as instructions or data. No MCP or clipboard bridge is documented, so this is not high, but the shared filesystem is enough for medium risk.
conditions: IF Agent A outputs documents into the same project directory that Agent B reads by default
IF Agent B parses file contents as trusted instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Separate A and B into different directories
Disable auto-ingest of newly written documents in B
Require provenance labels on A outputs before B reads them
Review any A-generated file before B processes it
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and provenance tracking between agents

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A is document-processing and Agent B has filesystem read plus broad network egress. If A touches sensitive documents and B can read the shared workspace, B may transmit those contents to external model providers or Plandex services. The profiles do not prove sensitive data classes, so medium is the highest supportable severity.
conditions: IF sensitive documents are placed in the shared project directory
IF Agent B sends file contents to its model provider or Plandex Cloud
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of B's workspace
Use a redacted copy for B
Disable network egress for B during sensitive tasks
Restrict B to a read-only subset of files
requires-engineering: enforce per-file data-loss prevention rules

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Agent B can write the filesystem and modify git state, while Agent A is a document processor with no write or coordination controls shown. In a shared project directory, B's default write behavior can overwrite or race with A's outputs, and git changes can become irreversible if applied incorrectly. Uncertainty about A's workspace isolation pushes this to high rather than medium.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same project directory
IF Agent B auto-applies edits while Agent A is still producing documents
mitigations: Run A and B in separate working trees
Disable auto-apply in B
Require manual review before git commits
Serialize access with a lock file
requires-engineering: add optimistic concurrency control for shared files

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent B's review-then-apply workflow can still treat upstream file content as authoritative if A's outputs are fed into B without verification. A is a document processor, so any extraction or transformation errors can cascade into B's edits or commits. The sandbox reduces blast radius, but default trust in upstream content keeps this at medium.
conditions: IF Agent A's extracted text is used as input to Agent B's plan
IF Agent B applies changes without independent verification
mitigations: Require B to cite source lines before acting
Add a human review step before apply
Compare A outputs against originals
Limit B to draft-only mode
requires-engineering: add automated verification against source documents

E_compliance.rationale: No specific regulated data class, residency mismatch, or retention policy is documented for either agent. A is document-processing and B handles source code plus model-provider API keys, so the only supportable compliance concern is a generic policy mismatch if regulated documents are introduced. The other agent is not cited because no concrete residency or certification gap is shown.
conditions: IF regulated documents are processed through the shared workspace
IF organizational policy forbids sending those documents to external model providers
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair
Use a local-only model path
Document retention and deletion rules
Review vendor terms before use
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing for regulated files
